AVALON CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  TUESDAY, FEBRUARY 18, 2025 5:00 PM  —

  410 AVALON CANYON ROAD
  AGENDA

  In compliance with the Americans with Disability Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this
  meeting, please contact the City Clerk’s Office (310) 510-0220. Notification 48 hours prior to the meeting will
  enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to this meeting. (28 CFR 35. 102-
  35.104 ADA Title II). All public records relating to an agenda item on this agenda are available for the public
  inspection at the time the records are distributed to all, or a majority of all, members of the City Council. Such
  records shall be available at City Hall located at 410 Avalon Canyon Rd.

For the public’s convenience, but not participation, the meeting can be viewed:
  On local cable: Catalina Broadband Solutions channel 3
  Streaming on Facebook Live: www.facebook.com/CityOfAvalonOfficial
  Streaming on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/CityofAvalonCA

CALL TO ORDER I PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE I INVOCATION I ROLL CALL

ANNOUNCEMENTS I WRITTEN COMMUNICATIONS

PRESENTATION

  1. Robert Greenlaw, CIP Director, will provide an update regarding the Five Corners
  Comprehensive Site Improvement Project.

DEPARTMENT HEAD REPORTS

CITY MANAGER REPORT I CITY ATTORNEY REPORT

COUNCILMEMBER REPORTSIREQUESTS I MAYOR REPORT

ORAL COMMUNICATION
Members of the public may address the City Council at this time. No action will be taken on non-
agenda items at this meeting. Speakers should limit comments to two (2) minutes each.

CONSENT CALENDAR

1.  City Council Minutes
  Although the live recording is the official record of public meetings, minutes are prepared
  for the Council’s approval.
  Recommended Action
  Approve minutes from the February 4, 2025 regular City Council Meetings.

2.  Warrants
  Expenditures Submitted for Approval
  • US Bank General Account Warrants totaling $399,340.27.
  • One payroll totaling $780,066.77.
  • Four electronic fund transfers totaling $192,367.90.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
FEBRUARY 18, 2025
PAGE 2

  Recommended Action
  Approve total expenditures for January 27, 2025 through February 7, 2025 totaling
  $849,272.14.

3.  FY25 Mid-Year Financial Results and Proposed Budget Amendments
  In June 2024, City Council adopted the City’s annual operating and capital budget for the
  fiscal year ending June 30, 2025. The unaudited revenue and expenditure figures for
  activity through December 31 have been compiled to provide a comparative update to the
  adopted budget.
  Recommended Action
  1. Receive the report of the Mid-Year Financial Results for FY24-25; and 2. Adopt a
  resolution authorizing the proposed budget amendments as outlined in Exhibit A to this
  report.

4.  Authorization to Provide On-Site Professionalized Services for the WWIP Pebbly Beach
  Lift Station Programmable Logic Controller
  PERC Water maintains the City’s Wastewater Treatment Plant, and have requested to
  have See Water Inc. rehabilitate Pebbly Beach Lift Station’s programmable logic
  controller. The rehabilitation requires installation of a new additional cabinet and control
  panel, CP1240-A, and moving sensitive wiring and components to the new control panel
  about 20 feet away from the sump area.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize PERC Water to contract See Water Inc. to provide on-site professionalized
  services for the WWTP Pebbly Beach Lift Station Programmable Logic Controller from
  Sewer Fund 108-25-652 1 for an amount of not-to-exceed $30,250.

5.  Reject Proposals Received for GIS Project
  The City has a Geographic Information Systems program managed with an outdated
  agreement. In December 2023, the City issued a request for proposal and received four
  proposals for GIS services in January 2024 ranging from $65,000 to over $500,000 for
  initial project implementation
  Recommended Action
  Reject proposals received for Geographic Information System (GIS) Services and
  Software Project.

GENERAL BUSINESS

6.  Magical Cruise Company Ltd Preferential Anchorage Access
  Magical Cruise Company Ltd, dba Disney Cruise Lines, has requested preferential
  access to the City’s anchorage point located outside of Avalon Harbor to support cruise
  ship operations. At this time, cruise ship anchorages are secured on a first requested,
  first secured basis. In order to secure preferential access, the City of Avalon and Disney
  Cruise Lines would establish a port agreement.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
FEBRUARY 18, 2025
PAGE 3

  Recommended Action
  1. Authorize the City Manager execute a Term Sheet with Magical Cruise Company Ltd,
  dba Disney Cruise Lines. 2. Authorize the City Manager to negotiate a Port Agreement
  with Magical Cruise Company Ltd, dba Disney Cruise Lines based on the terms set forth
  in the approved Term Sheet.

7.  Patrol Boat 4 Hull Repairs and Paint
  Patrol Boat 4 is part of a fleet of seven (7) boats necessary to carry out the day-to-day
  operations of the Harbor Department. The vessel is one of the primary patrol boats used
  in wintertime operations. After being taken to the mainland for an engine replacement, it
  was discovered to have some significant hull issues that need to be repaired.
  Recommended Action
  1. Make the affirmative finding that the City will not gain a competitive advantage by using
  the formal contract bid or other competitive procedure and dispense with formal bidding
  or other competitive procedures as outlined in Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-4.106.
  2. Authorize the City Manager to approve an expenditure not to exceed $30,000, from the
  Harbor Capital Improvement budget, account 10470-6781, for major repairs and
  refurbishment to be done to the hull of Patrol Boat 4.

8.  Green Pier Restroom Renovation Prolect
  The public restrooms at the Green Pier have been in use for approximately thirty years
  and are in need of significant upgrades to meet current standards of accessibility,
  hygiene, and aesthetics.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager, per the City’s purchasing policy, to execute an agreement
  with MKS Specialty Finishes, Inc., and Geoff King Plumbing, to perform renovation work
  to the public restrooms located at the Green Pier at a cost not to exceed $100,000 from
  the Green Pier Restrooms CIP fund (10470-6547) Project# 247005.

9.  Professional Services Agreement for Preliminary Site Assessment, Soil and Water
  Investigation, Corrective Action Plan and Verification Monitoring for Underground Storage
  Tank Site at the Ava Ion Fuel Dock
  The State of California requires closure of specific types of underground fuel storage by
  December 31, 2025. The City recently completed the removal of the four existing
  underground storage tanks at the Avalon Fuel Dock. The Los Angeles Regional Water
  Quality Control Board has requested a work plan and additional information from the
  City’s closure contractor.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize City Manager to negotiate and execute a Professional Service Agreement with
  Wayne Perry, Inc. for a not to exceed amount of $60,000 for Site Assessment, Soil and
  Water Investigation, Corrective Action Plan and Verification Monitoring for underground
  storage tank site at the Avalon Fuel Dock.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
FEBRUARY 18, 2025
PAGE 4

10.  Agreement with Los Angeles County for Participation in Los Angeles Region Imagery
  Acquisition Consortium Program and Geographic Information Systems Services
  The City of Avalon currently has a Geographic Information Systems (GIS) program
  managed with an outdated agreement. At the end of 2024, City staff met with Los Angeles
  County Internal Services Department GIS staff to inquire about services available to
  contract cities.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to execute a 3-year agreement with the County of Los
  Angeles for the City of Avalon’s participation in the Los Angeles Region Imagery
  Acquisition Consortium Program and assistance modernizing the City’s Geographic
  Information Systems environment in an amount not-to-exceed $115,000.

11.  Annual Financial Report for the Fiscal Year Ended June 30, 2024
  The annual financial report is the set of basic government financial statements that
  comply with the accounting requirements established by the Governmental Accounting
  Standards Board (GASB). The City’s financial statements were audited by Davis Farr
  LLP, an independent public accounting firm of licensed certified public accountants.
  Recommended Action
  Receive and file the annual financial report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024.

ADJOURN

NOTICE OF POSTING

I, Devin Elise Hart, declare that the City Council Agenda for Tuesday, February 18, 2025 was
posted  on  Friday,  February  14,  2025  on  the  City’s  website,
www.cityofavalon.com/aqendacenter, and at City Hall, 410 Avalon Canyon Road.

Devin Elise Hart, Senior Management Analyst

   AVALON CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  TUESDAY, FEBRUARY 4, 2025
  MINUTES

CALL TO ORDER: 5:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL- Present via Teleconference and In-Person: Mayor Anni Marshall,
Councilmembers Lisa Lavelle, Michael Ponce, Mary Schickling and Yesenia De La
Rosa. Also present: City Manager David Maistros, City Attorney Scott Campbell and
City Clerk Gabrielle Morones.

WRITTEN COMMUNICATIONS  -  None.

PRESENTATION

  1. Finance Director, Matthew Baker, provided a midyear review of the City’s Fiscal
  Year 2024-25 Budget.

CONSENT CALENDAR -There were 10 Items on the Consent Calendar. Item #10 was
pulled by Mayor Marshall for further discussion. Motion to approve Items #1-#9 made
by Lisa Lavelle, seconded by Lisa Lavelle, seconded by Mary Schickling. (All Ayes)

1.  City Council Minutes
  Approved minutes from the January 21, 2025 regular City Council Meetings.

2.  Warrants
  Approved US Bank General Account Warrants totaling $3,042,361.43, US Bank
  Housing Authority Warrants totaling $178,614.30, three payrolls totaling
  $780,066.77, five electronic fund transfers totaling $248,140.04 for a total
  expenditure of $4,249,182.54 for December 14, 2024 through January 24, 2025.

3.  Fiscal Year 2024-2025 Second Quarter Treasurer’s Report
  Adopted Resolution No. SA 25-03 of the City Council of the City of
  Avalon/Successor Agency to the Avalon Community Improvement Agency
  Adopting the Treasurer’s Investment Report for Fiscal Year 2024/2025 Second
  Quarter.

4.  City Manager Employment Agreement
  Authorized execution of the Employment Agreement for City Manager Services
  with David Maistros.

5.  Los Angeles County Public Health Services Contract
  Authorized the City Manager to execute the Los Angeles County Public Health
  Services Contract.
 CITY COUNCIL MINUTES
FEBRUARY 4, 2025
PAGE 2

6.  Resolution Approving the Blanket Authority to Apply for Grant Funds from the
  Los Angeles County Regional Park and Open Space District for Measure A
  Funding for Projects and Programs
  Adopted Resolution No. 25-04 of the City Council of the City of Avalon California
  Approving the Blanket Authority to File Applications for Grant Funds from the Los
  Angeles County Regional Park and Open Space District for Measure A Funding
  for Projects and Programs.

 7.  2025 Waterside Permit Renewals
  Authorized the Harbor Master to renew Waterside Permits for 2025.

8.  Professional Services Agreement for On-Call Planning Consultant
  Authorized the City Manager to negotiate and execute a professional services
  agreement with Sagecrest Planning and Environmental, LLC for on-call planning
  consultant services for a three-year term for an annual cumulative total not-to-
  exceed $150,000.00.

9.  Authorization to Provide On-Site Engineering and Support Services for WWTP
  Control System
  Authorized PERC Water to contract The LeMasters Company to provide on-site
  engineering and support services for the control system at the Wastewater
  Treatment Plant from Sewer Fund 108-25-652 1 for an amount of not-to-exceed
  $71,775.

PULLED ITEM  -  Pulled Item for further discussion.

10.  Global Paving RFP
  Authorized the City Manager or his designee(s) to develop and solicit a request
  for proposals from qualified firms to implement city-wide paving repairs.
  Motion to approve made by Michael Ponce, seconded by Anni Marshall.
  (All Ayes)

GENERAL BUSINESS

11.  Waterside Project Application  —Catalina Island Mermaids dba Avalon
  Barebottoms
  Made the affirmative finding that conditions set forth in the Avalon Municipal
  Code have been met and granted the Waterside Project Application to Catalina
  Island Mermaids, dba Avalon Barebottoms, with the following conditions: 1.
  Notification will be made to Harbor Office Personnel prior to dive operations
  being conducted. The Harbor Master retains the ability to restrict or curtail
  operations when conditions dictate. 2. Current registration for the skiff used in
  dive operations will be provided to the Harbor Master annually. 3. Skiff used in
 CITY COUNCIL MINUTES
FEBRUARY 4, 2025
PAGE 3

  dive operations wilt be secured to one of the public dinghy docks and meet all
  requirements for use of these docks. 4. Personnel conducting dives will have
  current and applicable professional certifications for dive operations and take all
  necessary safety precautions while operating within the Harbor. 5. Applicant will
  obtain a business license for Avalon Barebottoms separate from Catalina Island
  Mermaids LLC. This waterside permit applies to the conditions of use for Avalon
  Barebottoms. Activities related to Catalina Mermaids will begin and end from the
  shore. 6. Applicant abides by the Standard List of Conditions for Waterside
  Permit Holders.
  Motion to approve made by Michael Ponce, seconded by Lisa Lavelle. (All Ayes)

12.  Waterside Permit Application Island Enterprises, Inc. dba Catalina Adventure
  —

  Tours
  Made the affirmative finding that conditions set forth in the Avalon Municipal
  Code have been met and granted the Waterside Project Application to Island
  Enterprises, dba Catalina Tours, contingent upon the following conditions: 1.
  Allow Island Enterprises to utilize 1 non-exclusive use float in position “E” on the
  pier for their tour boat operation, utilizing the semisubmersible Nautilus (USCG
  documentation 1079045). The City will not charge fees for the float so long as its
  use is non-exclusive to Island Enterprises. 2. Allow occasional use of the Cabrillo
  Mole floats to pick up groups as long as Island Enterprises does not interfere with
  cross channel carriers or cruise ship traffic. 3. Require City Council approval if
  Island Enterprises elects to utilize their PUC Tariff on-call charter service to pick
  up passengers in all areas specified on the Tariff excluding services between any
  vessels, points and places starting with and ending within the Avalon city limits.
  4. If City Council approves at a later date, allow Island Enterprises on-call
  charters the ability to utilize any Green Pier float and allow occasional use of the
  Cabrillo Mole floats to pick up groups as long as Island Enterprises does not
  interfere with cross channel carriers or cruise ship traffic. 5. Require Island
  Enterprises to pay nightly mooring fees for their vessels.
  Motion to approve made by Lisa Lavelle, seconded by Yesenia De La Rosa.
  (All Ayes)

13.  Waterside Prolect Change Conditions of Use— Avalon Aquatic Excursions
  Made the affirmative finding that conditions set forth in the Avalon Municipal
  Code have been met and granted the Waterside Project Application to Avalon
  Aquatic Excursions, with the following conditions: 1. All operations to load and
  unload passengers will take place on Pleasure Pier floats with occasional use of
  the floats at the Cabrillo Mole. Applicant must not interfere with other commercial
  boat traffic including cross-town ferry and/or cruise ship tender traffic. During
  summer months applicant will make all efforts to utilize the shore-boat float of the
  End Float of the pier. 2. Applicant abides by the standard list of conditions for
  Waterside Permit holders. 3. Applicant meets all regulatory requirements for
 CITY COUNCIL MINUTES
FEBRUARY 4, 2025
PAGE 4

  passenger-carrying vessels of this type, including any U.S. Coast Guard and
  Public Utilities Commission requirements. 4. Prior to vessel acquisition, applicant
  will provide the Harbor Master with the technical specifications, including make,
  model, length, beam, propulsion type, passenger capacity for approval. Any
  future proposed changes to these specifications will require prior Harbor Master
  approval in writing.
  Motion to approve made by Michael Ponce, seconded by Lisa Lavelle. (All Ayes)

14.  City Vehicle Storage Yard Policy
  Approved the City of Avalon Vehicle Storage Yard Policy.
  Motion to approve made by Michael Ponce, seconded by Yesenia De La Rosa.
  (All Ayes)

15.  Introduction and First Reading of an Ordinance Repealing and Replacing Title 4,
  Public Safety, Chapter 4-1 Bicycles and Repealing Chapter 4-10 of the Avalon
  Municipal Code
  Introduced and waived all readings of an Ordinance of the City of Avalon
  Repealing and Replacing Title 4, Chapter 4-1 and Repealing Chapter 4-10 of the
  Avalon Municipal Code Regarding Bicycles, Electric Bicycles and Motorized
  Bicycles.
  Motion to approve made by Lisa Lavelle, seconded by Michael Ponce. (All Ayes)

Mayor Marshall adjourned the meeting at 6:44 p.m.

I, Gabrielle Morones, City Clerk, do hereby certify that the DVD videotape of the regular
City Council Meeting on February 4, 2025, is the official record of the Council Meeting
and is on file and maintained in City Hall.

Gabrielle Morones, City Clerk

BACKGROUND: On June 18, 2024, City Council adopted the City’s annual operating and
capital budget for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2025 (FY25). The adopted budget reflects
estimated General Fund revenues and transfers-in totaling $19.51 million comprised of operating
revenues totaling $12.84 million and grants and transfers totaling $6.67 million. General Fund
appropriations total $23.51, with recurring operating expenditures totaling $12.48, capital outlays
totaling $10.04 million and transfers to other funds totaling $995 thousand. Recurring revenues
exceed recurring expenditures by $361 thousand with reserves to be utilized to fund one-time
capital outlays. The adopted budget for the Harbor Fund includes fund revenues totaling $16.60
million, comprised of $9.22 million in operating revenues and $7.38 million in grants and other
non-operating revenues. Harbor Fund appropriations total $19.56 million with $8.44 million in
operating expenditures and $11.12 million in capital outlays. Similar to the General Fund,
recurring revenues exceed recurring expenditures, with reserves utilized to fund significant
capital outlays. Sewer, Saltwater, and Solid Waste Funds were budgeted to align with the cost
of service study adopted by City Council on June 1, 2021.

REPORT SUMMARY: The unaudited revenue and expenditure figures for activity through
December 31 have been compiled to provide a comparative update to the adopted budget. Due
to the timing of when certain revenues are received or when funds are expended (e.g. visitor-
driven revenues peak during first quarter, insurance premiums paid during first half of year),
amounts may be greater or less than 50% of the budgeted amounts as of December 3 1st. In
general, the report includes comparisons to the prior two fiscal years; however, the timing of
expenditures may vary from year-to-year impacting comparisons. The report is structured to
review operating revenues and expenditures separately from grants and capital outlays.

As part of the mid-year budget process, Management reviewed expenditures to identify accounts
where expenditures exceed or are on pace to exceed budgeted amounts. Proposed
amendments to the budget are requested in the report and outlined in Exhibit A. Under the City’s
Budget and Fiscal Policies adopted with the FY25 Budget, the City Manager has the authority
to make budget adjustments within departments and expenditure categories under certain

SUBJECT:  Authorization to Provide On-Site Professionalized Services
  for the WVVTP Pebbly Beach Lift Station Programmable
  Logic Controller

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize PERC Water to contract See Water Inc. to
provide on-site professionalized services for the WWTP Pebbly Beach Lift Station
Programmable Logic Controller from Sewer Fund 108-25-6521 for an amount of not-to-
exceed $30,250.

REPORT SUMMARY: PERC Water maintains the City’s Wastewater Treatment Plant
(WWTP), and have requested to have See Water Inc. rehabilitate Pebbly Beach Lift
Station’s programmable logic controller. The rehabilitation requires installation of a new
additional cabinet and control panel, CP1240-A, and moving sensitive wiring and
components to the new control panel about 20 feet away from the sump area. The existing
cabinet and control panel are extremely close to the sump area and exposed to high
levels of H2S gas, which is causing abnormal deterioration of the current control circuit
components. The improvements are needed to maintain operational efficiency and
compliance with State regulatory permit requirements. The proposed scope of work
coincides with the work The LeMasters Company is completing, which ensures seamless
operations of the whole WWTP system.

PERC Water has requested to engage See Water Inc. to perform the following scope of
work:
  1. Remove all sensitive electronics, e.g., PLC, HMI, Modbus gateway, and all
  other door mounted components from the existing control cabinet and these
  components will be re-installed into a new control panel, CP1240-A.
  2. Replace all control wires (12OVAC/24VDC), with new wires.
  3. All new wires to be coated in corrosion resistant grease with ferrule connectors.
  4. New stainless steel enclosure with lockable latch and dead front inner door to
  be installed about 20 feet away from sump area.
  5. Includes Terminal Blocks to wire PLC connections, pump portal remote
  monitoring equipment and online service.
 FISCAL IMPACTS: A cost not-to-exceed $30,250. Sufficient funds exist in FY 24-25
Sewer Fund 108-25-6521.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Improved efficiency and reliability of plant operations.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: Would delay
critical upgrades to the WWTP Pebbly Beach Lift Station control system, potentially
effecting plant operations and overflow, and possible lift station failure.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Authorize PERC Water to contract See Water Inc.to perform on-
site professionatized services for the WWTP Pebbly Beach Lift Station Programmable
Logic Controller as requested.

continue to have an open RFP file.

SUBJECT:  Magical Cruise Company Ltd Preferential Anchorage Access

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Authorize the City Manager to execute the Term Sheet
with Magical Cruise Company Ltd, dba Disney Cruise Lines. 2. Authorize the City
Manager to negotiate a Port Agreement with Magical Cruise Company Ltd, dba Disney
Cruise Lines incorporating the terms set forth in the approved Term Sheet.

REPORT SUMMARY: Magical Cruise Company Ltd, dba Disney Cruise Lines, has
expressed its desire to enter into a port agreement establishing, among other terms, an
allowance for defined scheduling dates in the City of Avalon. Currently there is no written
policy regarding the scheduling of cruise ship anchorage requests.

In order to secure access to preferred dates, the City of Avalon and Disney Cruise Lines
would establish a port agreement. A proposed port agreement would include the following
terms as set forth in a formal Term Sheet:
  -  Initial term length of five years, with two additional five-year options.
  -  Preferential scheduling for Saturdays and Tuesdays during the “Peak Season”
  (September 15 to May 15).
  -  Preferential scheduling for Tuesdays during the “Summer Season” (May 16 to
  September 14).
  -  Disney Cruise Lines shall guarantee a minimum of 120,000 passenger visits to the
  City per year.
  o In the event of a shortfall in any given year, Disney Cruise Lines will remit
  payment at the current wharfage rate.
  -  Disney Cruise Lines proposes to remit the current wharfage rate ($7.50 per person
  for each passenger on the manifest) plus an additional $1.50 per person as
  consideration for preferential scheduling.
  o This rate will be subject to annual adjustments equal to 2.5% per year.

At this time, Disney Cruise Lines has two vessels on the West Coast Disney Magic and
  —

Disney Wonder. Both vessels have a maximum passenger capacity of approximately
2,700 passenger. Though these vessels are approximately half the capacity of some of
the cruise ships that currently visit Avalon on Tuesdays, the proposed increased wharfage
rate is anticipated to offset any potential loss of wharfage revenue associated with
diminished passenger counts. Additionally, smaller capacity ships may provide an overall
more enjoyable experience for passengers as well as other Island visitors and residents.
 The reduced crowds will result in less congestion, greater activity opportunities, and
quicker queuing at the Cabrillo Mole.

The proposed Term Sheet establishes a requirement for Disney Cruise Lines to submit a
berthing schedule eighteen (18) months prior to that start of either season  Peak or
  —

Summer. If any Tuesday and/or Saturday are not booked by Disney Cruise Lines within
18 months prior to the start of the season in question, the date may reserved by another
cruise line.

In addition to increased wharfage and a guaranteed minimum passenger count, Disney
Cruise Lines also has offered to work collaboratively with the City to identify areas of
opportunity or need and provide support and expertise to assist the City in developing
strategies regarding design and engineering services, industrial engineering services,
quality guest service culture and processes training, and operational efficiency analysis.
The exact scope of services to be provided will be formally memorialized either in the final
port agreement, or by separate agreement(s) to be approved by the City Council.

City Staff recommends the City Council authorize the City Manager to execute the
attached Term Sheet with Disney Cruise Lines and further, authorize the City Manager to
negotiate the terms of a port agreement with Magical Cruise Company Ltd, dba Disney
Cruise Lines. The final port agreement will be brought back before the City Council for
formal approval.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Staff anticipate the action may have a net neutral effect on future
fiscal year wharfage revenue projections.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City of
Avalon will not have a port agreement with Disney Cruise Lines.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Negotiate an agreement to bring back to the City Council for
approval.

SUBJECT:  Patrol Boat 4 Hull Repairs and Paint

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Make the affirmative finding that the City will not gain a
competitive advantage by using the formal contract bid or other competitive procedure and
dispense with formal bidding or other competitive procedures as outlined in Avalon Municipal
Code Section 3-4.106. 2. Authorize the City Manager to approve an expenditure not to exceed
$30,000, from the Harbor Capital Improvement budget, account 10470-6781, for major repairs
and refurbishment to be done to the hull of Patrol Boat 4.

REPORT SUMMARY: Patrol Boat 4 is part of a fleet of seven (7) boats necessary to carry out
the day-to-day operations of the City of Avalon Harbor Department. It is one of the primary
patrol boats used in wintertime operations. After being taken to the mainland for an engine
replacement, it was discovered to have some significant hull issues that need to be repaired as
soon as possible. These repairs will extend the useful life of the boat for several years.

Basin Marine has provided an estimate of $25,955 to complete the project and they are able to
start the job immediately.

Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-4.106 requires a competitive process be implemented for
procurements greater than $25,000. However, AMC Section 3-4.111 (c) allows for exceptions
for bidding or other competitive procedures for economic efficiency. Per the AMC:

  If a competitive market does not exist, or the City will not gain a competitive advantage
  by using the formal contract bid or other competitive procedure, or where the public
  projec1, goods or services may be obtained more economically or efficiently without the
  procedure, the City may dispense with formal bidding or other competitive procedures.

It would also be economically efficient to have the work done at Basin Marine, where the boat
is currently located. It would require substantial additional costs to transport the boat to three
different vendors to meet the requirement of three competitive bids.

Additionally, due to the importance of this boat for wintertime operations an urgent condition
exists to have the hull repairs done as quickly as possible.

Staff recommends the City Council makes the affirmative finding that the City will not gain a
competitive advantage by using the formal contract bid or other competitive procedure and
dispense with formal bidding or other competitive procedures as outlined in Avalon Municipal
Code Section 3-4.106. Staff also recommends the City Council authorizes the City Manager to
approve an expenditure not to exceed $30,000, from the Harbor Capital Improvement budget,
 account 10470-6781, for major repairs and refurbishment to be done to the hull of Patrol Boat
4

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Fleet management.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Major repairs to patrol boats were anticipated in the adopted Fiscal Year
2024-25 Budget for Vehicle Replacement, 10470-6781.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: Harbor Department
personnel will not have an essential piece of equipment for winter-time operations.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implement City Council direction.

SUBJECT:  Green Pier Restroom Renovation Project

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager, per the City’s purchasing policy, to
execute an agreement with MKS Specialty Finishes, Inc., and Geoff King Plumbing, to perform
renovation work to the public restrooms located at the Green Pier at a cost not to exceed
$100,000 from the Green Pier Restrooms CIP fund (10470-6547) Project #247005.

REPORT SUMMARY: The public restrooms at the Green Pier have been in use for
approximately thirty years and are in need of significant upgrades to meet current standards of
accessibility, hygiene, and aesthetics. The restrooms serve a high volume of residents and
tourists, making their renovation a priority for maintaining the city’s reputation and ensuring
public comfort and safety.

This project was identified as a priority by City Staff and $100,000 was budgeted in CIP Project
#247005, Fund 10470-6547 for Fiscal Year 2025-26. However, due to increased levels of need,
the project has been scheduled to be completed before the end of the current Fiscal Year. Per
the City’s adopted Budget and Fiscal Policies:

“For transfers under $100,000, City Manager approval is required for transfers between capital
projects in the same year and same fund.”

To fund this project, the City Manager has authorized a transfer from Capital Improvement
Project #180049  — Green Pier Repairs. This project has the same fund as the Green Pier
Restrooms Project (10470-6547) as well as $450,000 budgeted this Fiscal Year.

The renovation will include the installation of new toilet partitions, urinal screens, and improved
lighting throughout both restrooms. This work is to be done by our Public Works staff. The
flooring in the women’s restroom is still in relatively good condition, but the men’s restroom
flooring is in need of replacement. MKS Specialty Finishes will install new concrete flooring in
men’s restroom, which will include reinforcing the existing subflooring. All new toilets are to be
installed in both restrooms by Geoff King, with help from Public Works. During construction,
temporary restroom facilities will be provided to minimize inconvenience to the public. Efforts will
be made to ensure that disruption is kept to a minimum.
 MKS Specialty Finishes and Geoff King Plumbing were selected based on their extensive
experience with similar projects, competitive pricing, and positive references. Quotes were
requested from two other local contractors. Both Straight Up Builders and Elias Garcia
Construction reviewed the project, but declined to provide a quote. This fulfills the competitive
process purchasing procedure requirement specified in the Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-
4.106(a).

It is recommended that the City Council authorize the City Manager to execute contracts with
MKS Specialty Finishes, Inc., and Geoff King Plumbing, to complete the renovation of the public
restrooms at the Green Pier, with a total project budget not to exceed $100,000. Authorizing
these contracts will allow for the timely and efficient renovation of the public restrooms at the
Green Pier, enhancing the facility for all users and ensuring compliance with modern standards.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Allocate $100,000 from Green Pier Restrooms CIP fund (10470-6547)
Project # 247005 to allow the renovation project to be performed.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: Continued use of
outdated and deteriorating restroom facilities may lead to increased maintenance costs and
more frequent repairs, further straining the city’s resources. Residents and tourists may continue
to express dissatisfaction with the state of the restrooms, impacting the city’s reputation as a
desirable destination.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implement City Council direction.

agenda pursuant to the Brown Act.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S):  Authorize City Manager to negotiate and execute a

for Site Assessment, Soil and Water Investigation, Corrective Action Plan and Verification
Monitoring for underground storage tank site at the Avalon Fuel Dock.

REPORT SUMMARY: The State of California requires the owners or operators of specific
types of underground fuel storage tanks to permanently close by December 31, 2025. In
response to that requirement the City just recently completed the removal of the four existing
underground storage tanks at the Avalon Fuel Dock. As part of the removal process the open
excavation was tested for regulated contaminates, then the excavation was backfilled after an
initial consultation with regulatory agencies along with the replacement of the concrete
surfacing. Subsequent processing and analysis of the test results was then distilled into a
closure report that made its way through several regulatory agencies over the subsequent few
months following the site closure.

The closure report was first reviewed by the Los Angeles County, Department of Public Works
(LADPW) under their Underground Storage Tank (UST) program. If LADPW was satisfied that
the site was clean then it could file a favorable report with the Los Angeles Regional Water
Quality Control Board (LARWQCB), the agency responsible surface and ground water quality
in Los Angeles County. If there are some concerns with the results of the closure report, then
LADPW transmits their concerns to the LARWQCB which then opens a case and requests
corrective actions. In the case of the Avalon Fuel Dock, the Board requested a work plan and
additional information from the City’s closure contractor. The request was based on information
in the closure report that stated that a portion of the test results showed that site had been
impacted with petroleum constituents and the extent of the constituents had not been fully
delineated.

Wayne Perry, Inc. was the City’s fuel station contractor for the UST removal project and also
for the project to connect the new replacement above ground storage tank (AST). They were
responsible for the Closure Report preparation and follow-up with the agencies to facilitate the
closure to this point. Wayne Perry is intimately aware of the details of the fuel facilities at the
Avalon Fuel Dock. In addition to the UST and AST projects, Wayne Perry was the fuel station
subcontractor for the reconstruction of the Avalon Fuel Dock and the seasonal fuel float
project. Considering their background knowledge and expertise with the Avalon Fuel Dock,
 City staff requested a proposal for the Work Plan scope as they are the most knowledgeable
and qualified to provide the services efficiently as they are already fully engaged with the

Site Assessment Work Plan

In the Work Plan, WPI proposes advancing five soil borings to delineate soil and
groundwater impacts beneath the Site. During UST removal activities in May 2024,
groundwater was encountered at approximately 10 feet below ground surface (bgs). Due
to the Site’s proximity to Avalon Bay, the depth to groundwater likely varies with the tides.
WPI anticipates encountering groundwater between 10 and 15 feet bgs. The borings will
be advanced to a depth of approximately 20 feet bgs, or five feet below first encountered
groundwater, using a direct push drill rig. Soil samples will be collected every five feet
and preserved for laboratory analysis via Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
Method 5035. The soil will be field screened using a photo-ionization detector (PID) and
visually examined for soil classification. A 10-foot temporary screen will be placed into
each boring and will be set at the total depth. Groundwater samples will be collected at
each boring using a pencil bailer. Soil and groundwater samples will be analyzed for total
petroleum hydrocarbons as gasoline (TPHg) and total petroleum hydrocarbons as diesel
(TPHd) by EPA Method 8015M, and for benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, total xylenes
(collectively, BTEX), and fuel oxygenates by EPA Method 8260B. Following soil and
groundwater sampling activities, the borings will be backfilled with neat cement grout and
capped with concrete.

In 2016, a case (Avalon Fuel Dock; Global ID No. Ti 0000009443) was previously referred

in-place. The soil samples were collected at a maximum depth of 5 feet below ground
surface (bgs). The soil samples indicated maximum concentrations of total petroleum
hydrocarbons (TPH) at 100 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg), diesel range organics (DRO)
at 170 mg/kg, and toluene at 0.014 mg/kg. In August 2016, ten additional soil samples were
collected beneath the product piping associated with four other USTs (two 4,000-gallon
gasoline USTs, one 4,000-gallon diesel UST, and one 3,000-gallon pre-mixed fuel UST).
The soil samples were collected at a total depth of 4.5 feet bgs. Soil samples indicated a

Other constituents were not detected above their respective reporting limits. Groundwater
was not encountered during soil sampling activities. On October 24, 2016, a non-case letter
was issued by the Los Angeles Water Board.

(PID) was used to monitor volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in the excavated soil. PID
readings did not exceed 50 parts per million (ppm) during excavation activities. Soil and
groundwater samples were analyzed for total petroleum hydrocarbons as gasoline (TPHg)
and TPHd by Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Method 8015B; full-scan VOCs,
including benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, total xylenes (collectively BTEX), and methyl
tertiary butyl ether (MTBE), by EPA Method 8260B; and lead by HMU-900.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager to execute a 3-year
agreement with the County of Los Angeles for the City of Avalon’s participation in the Los
Angeles Region Imagery Acquisition Consortium Program and assistance modernizing
the City’s Geographic Information Systems environment in an amount not-to-exceed
$115,000.

REPORT SUMMARY: The City of Avalon currently has a Geographic Information
Systems (GIS) program managed with an outdated agreement. At the end of 2024, City
staff met with Los Angeles County Internal Services Department GIS staff to inquire about
services available to contract cities. City staff from Public Works, Planning, Information
Technology, and the City Manager’s Office met with the County team to discuss services.
The County shared information about the Los Angeles Region Imagery Acquisition
Consortium Program (LARIAC) which provides high-resolution aerial orthogonal and
oblique imagery (including building outlines and digital terrain), immediate access to
Connect Explorer GIS viewer (including parcel data, streets, and addresses), licenses for
City staff, and training. The high-resolution imagery is updated every (3) years (last
collected in 2023). LARIAC participants include over 30 County departments, and 40
additional partner organizations including municipalities, other public agencies, and
academic institutions.

In addition, Los Angeles County can provide services related to modernizing the City’s
GIS system. This support includes initial analysis, evaluation, data migration, and project
management for implementing a new software program. The software program and all
associated data will be owned by the City of Avalon. If needed, City staff will return to City
Council for the procurement of the new software program upon initial analysis of Los
Angeles County staff.

Both participation in LARIAC and a modern GIS program could be invaluable tools for
Planning, Building, Public Works, Public Safety, and Administration in helping staff map,
analyze, and understand spatial data. Updating the City’s GIS can improve management
of urban planning, emergency response, transportation and traffic, parcel data,
environmental data, or infrastructure maintenance. In addition, with key stakeholders
 participating in LARIAC the City of Avalon would benefit tremendously from sharing
mapping and aerial data as would our public safety partners.

The LARIAC program is a one of a kind consortium with a variety of local participants,
including those specific to the island including Los Angeles County Departments (ex.
Sheriff, Fire, Planning), Santa Catalina Island Conservancy, and Southern California
Edison. In addition, the experience the County staff have with GIS services is unique to
LA County layers, property data, and experience providing many of those services
already on Santa Catalina Island.

Therefore, to ensure compatibility with existing data sets, to take advantage of LA County
experience, and to piggyback off aerial data collection efforts already occurring on Santa
Catalina Island, it is recommended to enter into an agreement with Los Angeles County
to participate in LARIAC and for services related to GIS modernization utilizing AMC 3-4-
.11(c) Economic Efficiency. LARIAC is a consortium of existing multi-jurisdictional
agreements that enable local governments to efficiently and cost-effectively acquire high
definition aerial data. Due to the fact the County is already collecting and mapping data
for the unincorporated portions of the Island through the LARIAC program, the City can
expect gained economic efficiency by awarding this agreement.

FISCAL IMPACTS: There is currently $30,000 in the FY2024/25 general operating
budget for services related to GIS which will cover year one of the agreement and
software licensing.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Improved business processes.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City will
continue to have an outdated GIS program.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Execute an agreement with Los Angeles County.

posted agenda pursuant to the Brown Act.

Overview of Data Acquisition Process  —  LARIAC 7

EagleView acquired ortho and oblique imagery for the LARIAC 7 Project. Aerial
photography data were collected and processed by EagleView for all LARIAC 7
project areas. The collected nadir image chips were post processed by
EagleView.

To provide the proper geodetic controls for the production of the digital ortho
imagery, a combination of existing GPS ground control points and GPS/IMU were
employed during the image capture. Existing digital terrain model (DTM) data
from LARIAC6 was provided by Los Angeles County and used in the production
of the digital ortho imagery. EagleView accomplished aerial triangulation (AT
solution) of the photo set using automatic analytical aerial triangulation (AAAT)
procedures in a softcopy environment and the resulting external orientations.

EagleView processed the imagery, completed the orthorectification and produced
4-band (RGBNIR), 32-bit (8-bit per channel) digital orthophotos at 4-inch and 9-
inch pixel resolution for respective project areas with no overlap between areas.
The 4-inch (0.32’ final pixel size) and 9-inch (0.8’ final pixel size) areas were color
balanced independently. The ground resolution of the ortho photography will be
approximately nominal 10 cm GSD (Ground Sample Distance) and nominal 28
cm GSD. All products from the LARIAC 7 Project underwent rigorous quality
assurance and quality control (QA/QC) procedures by Dewberry Engineers Inc.
(hereafter referred to as Dewberry) as an independent QAIQC firm.

All project data were established and produced in the NAD 83 (2011) California
State Plane Coordinate System (1983, Zone V). The 4-inch and 9-inch pixel
resolution orthophotos were delivered by EagleView to Dewberry for eventual
distribution to the LARIAC 7 participants. Oblique imagery was delivered by
EagleView to Dewberry for eventual distribution to the LARIAC 7 participants.

Horizontal and Vertical Positional Accuracy

Horizontal Accuracy  —  For Orthophotos
LARIAC 7’s 4” digital orthophotos were tested in accordance with the 4 inch GSD
Acceptance Criteria. The “georeferenced ground positions of higher accuracy,”
referred to generically as “QAIQC checkpoints,” were provided from the first
LARIAC project and from other data points collected by the vendors. The
National Standard for Spatial Data Accuracy (NSSDA) absolute accuracy statistic
(Accuracyr) is computed as RMSEr x 1 .7308 in order to report the tested
horizontal accuracy at the 95% confidence level as required by FGDC Geospatial
Positioning Accuracy Standards, Part 3: NSSDA. The 4” digital orthophotos were
tested with 0.91 feet horizontal accuracy at 95% confidence level. Class 1 (1
foot accuracy) for Area 1 and 3 and class 2 (2 foot accuracy) are the same
standards as LARIAC.

Horizontal and Vertical Positional Accuracy  -  For Oblique Imagery
The georeferenced ground positions of higher accuracy, referred to generically as
QA/QC checkpoints, were provided by LARIAC 7 from multiple sources. Most
checkpoints were X’s painted on asphalt, accurately surveyed as control points,
and used as target points by photogrammetric firms for aerial triangulation.
Because these checkpoints are accurate, well defined and photo-identifiable on
the airborne oblique imagery, Dewberry measured the x-, y- and z-coordinates on
these checkpoints on each of the 4-view Eagle View images, where visible, to
compute errors in Eastings (ax), errors in Northings (Ay), and errors in elevations
(Az). For each checkpoint, Dewberry also averaged the Eastings, Northings and
elevations for all views that were visible; for many, the average resulted from four
views, but some points were obscured by buildings, trees, cars, etc., so the
average resulted from the mean of three, two, and (in a few cases) only one view.

west-view images, the averaged coordinates were normally more accurate than

City of Avalon Profile

The City of Avalon is the only incorporated community located on Santa Catalina Island in the
Channel Islands, approximately twenty-two miles off the coast of Southern California. The
City is situated on the leeward side of the island around Avalon Bay and its jurisdictional
boundaries occupy just under three square miles or approximately 3.8% of the entire island.
The City serves a population of approximately 3,300 residents and welcomes over one million
visitors each year through its picturesque harbor, with the majority of residents and visitors
arriving through the City’s Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal.

The City of Avalon is located entirely within the coastal zone and the local economy is centered
on tourism. As the majority of the City is already built-out, new development primarily comes
from infill which helps to preserve the compact, walkable character of the City. The autoette,
which is smaller and travels at lower speeds compared to traditional automobiles, is the most
common method of transportation in the City and the City closely regulates both the size and
number of vehicles permitted to facilitate congestion and encourage active transportation.
The City’s Green Pleasure Pier serves as the hub for commercial and recreational ocean-based
activities, including fishing, scuba diving, parasailing and kayaking. In addition to the natural
open space areas, the City offers multiple parks, picnic areas, and public beaches for both
residents and visitors to enjoy.

Form of Government

Incorporated on June 26, 1913, as a general law city, the City operates under the Council-
Manager form of government with a five-member City Council elected by the citizens. The
Mayor is directly elected to serve a two-year term and Council Members are elected at large
to alternating four-year terms. The City Council serves as the legislative and policy-making
body of the City, enacting laws and directing such actions as required to provide for the
general welfare of the community. The City Manager, appointed by the City Council, is
responsible for the administration of all City affairs and the implementation of all policies and
ordinances established by the City Council. The City Attorney serves under contract and is
appointed by the City Council. All other staff are appointed by the City Manager.

As a full-service city, Avalon provides its citizens with fire protection, planning, public works,
recreation, and community services. The City contracts law enforcement services through the
Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department. In addition to these governmental services, the
City is responsible for providing harbor, sewer, saltwater, solid waste, and transit services
which are managed as proprietary or business-like activities. Harbor operations include the
assignment of moorings, patrol and enforcement of state and local laws, administration of
waterside business permits, scheduling of dock usage for commercial passenger vessels, and
the maintenance of harbor facilities. Sewer and solid waste operations are managed by the
 Cty uti!iz!ng contcicted service provkie to operate the City-owned waste-water tratmenL
pl:nt and landfill, respectiveiy. In addton, due to the limited freshwater resources on the
island, the City utilizes a saltwater system as tnc water supply source for sewer and fire
suppression. Lastly, during the fiscal year, the City implemented a new on-demand, app-
based, point-to-point shuttle transit system utilizing a contractor to provide low-cost
transportation to residents and visitors anywhere within the City limits which replaced a
contracted fixed route bus and dial-a-ride transit service.

Budgetary Process and Controls

The City’s budgetary records are maintained on a modified accrual basis, which means that
revenues are recorded when measurable and available and expenditures are recorded when
goods and services are received or when liability is incurred. The City produces an annual
budget, which serves as the foundation for the City of Avalon’s financial planning and control.
Based on the City of Avalon’s Budget and Fiscal Policies, the City is required to adopt a
structurally balanced budget, where current operating expenditures are paid with recurring
revenues, which are estimated utilizing conservative and transparent assumptions, and one
time revenues are used only to support capital outlays and other non-recurring expenditures.

City Staff considers the goals and priorities of the City Council during the budget development
process and the Finance Director presents drafts of the budget to the City Council at public
workshops held during the months of May and June. After public input and discussion is
received, the City Manager will recommend the budget for adoption and the City Council may
request further modifications or introduce an ordinance adopting the budget. The City’s
budget is then adopted by ordinance and becomes effective on July 1st of each fiscal year.
Expenditures authorized in the final budget ordinance are appropriated at the fund level, and
in the case of the General Fund, at the department or program level. All amendments to the
budget at these levels can only be approved by the City Council. The City Manager has the
authority to transfer funds within a given fund and between department appropriations to
ensure that programmatic budgets may adapt throughout the year to evolving circumstances,
as outlined in the City’s Budget and Fiscal Policies.

All governmental, enterprise, and internal service funds are appropriated annually. The
governmental funds include the General Fund and special revenue funds, including the
Housing Authority, Local Transportation, and other non-major governmental funds.

Current Economic Conditions and Outlook

The information presented in the financial statements can be better understood when it is
considered from the broader perspective of the environment in which the City operates. The
City of Avalon’s local economy is centered on tourism and the City offers various attractions
and activities to its visitors which take advantage of the City’s picturesque landscapes, mild
climate, and vibrant waterfront shopping and dining district. The City’s operations are largely
funded through visitor-driven tax revenues and fees, including Transient Occupancy Tax
(TOT), Sales Tax, and Wharfage Fees on cross channel and cruise ship passengers.

Transient Occupancy Tax (TOT)
TOT is the City’s largest source of revenue, with $7.8 million representing approximately
47.4°k of all General Fund revenues for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024. The City’s TOT
revenues are generated from a 12% tax on both commercial hotels and short-term vacation
rentals. The City allocates 22% of the TOT collected to the Love Catalina Island Tourism
Authority to be used for the promotion of the City, as approved by the voters in April 2004.

In response to the pandemic, restrictions on non-essential travel during the last quarter of
the Fiscal Year 2019-20 reduced TOT revenues to approximately $4.5 million, which was down
$893 thousand or 16.6% from the prior year. With the easing of restrictions during Fiscal Year
2020-21, the City’s abundance of open spaces and proximity to large urban population centers
allowed the City to take advantage of pent-up demand for travel with TOT revenues
rebounding to approximately $6.0 million, on track with pre-pandemic trends. In Fiscal Year
2021-22, TOT revenues increased significantly from historical levels, reaching $8.7 million.
The increase was attributed to increased average room rates as room occupancy rates and
the number of rooms available did not increase by enough to account for the increase in
revenue. During the fiscal year ended June 30, 2023, revenues decreased 4.4% to
approximately $8.3 million, with the decrease attributed to an unusually wet winter season
impacting visitor levels during the second half of the year. TOT revenues experienced another
moderate decline of 5.4% to $7.8 million during the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024, with a
rare tropical storm in August 2023 prompting an evacuation of the island during the peak
visitor season contributing to the decrease. The table below summarizes TOT revenues by
source over the past ten fiscal years. A ten year comparison of all tax revenues can be found
in the Statistical Section beginning on page 117 of this report.

On August 1, 2023, the City Council voted unanimously to establish, by urgency ordinance, a
45 day moratorium on the issuance of any transient rental licenses to persons who submitted
an application following the effective date of the ordinance. The temporary moratorium was
issued to protect existing housing stock and allow the City time to study appropriate
regulations to maintain public safety and the health of the community, as well as ensure that
the issuance of these licenses does not undermine the City’s affordable housing goals. The
moratorium does not prevent those who have already been issued a license from continuing
to operate transient rentals under those entitlements. The City Council voted unanimously to
extend the urgency ordinance for up to 10 months and 15 days on September 15, 2023.
During the fiscal year, the City held several public stakeholder meetings and conducted a
survey to provide additional insight and community input. On August 6, 2024, the City Council
voted unanimously to further extend the moratorium to July 30, 2025, to provide additional
time for analysis and development of further regulations. While revenues from transient
rentals decreased during the fiscal year, the decrease was not attributable to the moratorium
considering similar decreases were experienced in revenues from hotels over the same period.
While the moratorium is not anticipated to have a significant effect on TOT revenues in the
short-term, any long-term impacts on revenue growth will be considered as part of the
analysis performed.

harbor operating revenues. Wharfage fees are charged to cruise ships and cross channel
carriers on a per passenger basis for their use of or impact upon City harbor facilities. The $3
per cross channel passenger fee and $5 per cruise ship passenger fee was unchanged from
the prior fiscal year. Combined wharfage revenues totaled $5.78 million, up 6.7% from the
prior fiscal year. The increase in revenues was attributable to increased visitors from cruise

up $9 thousand or 0.2%. While the one hundred and sixteen (116) cruise ship arrivals was
comparable to pre-pandemic averages, the average number of passengers on board has
increased to approximately 3,200 passengers with cruise operators transitioning to larger
vessels since resuming operations after the pandemic. The increase in average occupancy is
anticipated to continue into the next fiscal year as three cruise ships with occupancy limits in
excess of 5,000 passengers arrived in the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024, and seventeen
(17) are scheduled to arrive during the fiscal year ending June 30, 2025.

Five Corners Pedestrian Improvement Project
The Five Corners Pedestrian Improvement Project is a complete streets design improvement
to the intersections of Tremont Street, Avalon Canyon Road, Country Club Drive, and Sumner
Avenue. The $5.8 million project is primarily funded by grants including funds from Local
Transportation Funds through the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority
(Metro), State of California’s State Active Transportation Grant through the California
Transportation Commission (CTC), and a local match from the City which includes the City’s
Senate Bill (SB) 1 annual allocation derived from fuel taxes and vehicle fees. During the fiscal
year ended June 30, 2024, the City pursued additional grant funding opportunities and was
awarded approximately $3.2 million from CTC on April 8, 2024. The goal of the project is to
provide safer transportation access along Tremont Avenue and through the “Five Corners”
intersection, with improvements including new sidewalks, public transit stops, safer crossings,
traffic calming, landscape beautification, and wayfinding.

reported as net position. Certain interfund activities have been eliminated as required by
GASB Statement No. 34. Over time, increases or decreases in net position may serve as a
useful indicator of whether the financial position of the City is improving or deteriorating. In
order to assess the overall health or financial condition of the City, other non-financial factors
should also be taken into consideration which include changes in the City’s property tax base
and the condition of the City’s infrastructure (roads, improvements, drainage, storm and
sewer lines, etc.).

The Statement of Activities presents information showing how the City’s net position changed
during the most recent fiscal year. All changes in net position are reported as soon as the
underlying event giving rise to the change occurs, regardless of the timing of related cash
flows. This is consistent with a full accrual concept, which may result in the reporting of
revenues and expenses in the current fiscal year, with cash flows occurring in future fiscal
periods (e.g. uncollected revenues, pension contributions, and earned but not used leave).

Both government-wide financial statements distinguish functions of the City that are
principally supported by taxes and intergovernmental revenues (governmental activities)
from other functions that are intended to recover all or a significant portion of their costs
through user fees and charges (business-type activities). All of the City’s basic services are
considered governmental activities. This includes general government, public safety, public
works, building and planning, and community services. These services are supported by
general City revenues such as taxes, and by specific program revenues such as ambulance
charges and recreation program fees. The City’s business-type activities include harbor,
sewer, salt water, solid waste, and transit operations. Unlike governmental activities, these
services are to be supported by charges paid by users based on the amount of services used.

The government-wide financial statements can be found on page 26 of this report.

 Fund T[ranciaI Statrncnts

A fund is a grouping of reiated accounts that s used to nantn control over resources that
have been seqregated for specific activities or objectives. Th City, ike other state and local
governments, uses fund accounting to ensure and dernonstate compliance with finance-
related legal requirements for using certain taxes, grants, and other resources.

Fund financial statements provide detailed information about each of the City’s most
significant funds, called major funds. Major funds are presented individually, with all non-
major funds summarized and presented in a single column. Subordinate schedules present
the detail of these non-major funds. Major funds present the major activities of the City for
the fiscal year and may change from year to year as a result of changes in the pattern of the
City’s activities. The City’s funds are segregated into three categories: Governmental Funds,
Proprietary Funds, and Fiduciary Funds.

Governmental Funds are used to account for essentially the same functions reported as
governmental activities in the government-wide financial statements. However, unlike the
government-wide financial statements, governmental funds focus on near-term inflows and
outflows of spendable resources, as well as on balances of spendable resources available at
the end of the fiscal year. This represents a modified accrual basis of accounting, with capital
assets, long-lived assets, and long-term liabilities excluded from the financial statements.
Such information may be useful in evaluating the City’s near-term financing requirements.

Because the focus of governmental funds is narrower than that of the government-wide
financial statements, it is useful to compare the information presented for the governmental
funds with similar information presented for governmental activities in the government-wide
financial statements. By doing so, readers may better understand the long-term impact of the
government’s near-term financing decisions. Both the governmental fund balance sheet and
the governmental fund statement of revenues, expenditures and changes in fund balances
provide a reconciliation to facilitate the comparison between governmental funds and
governmental activities.

The major governmental funds include the General Fund, Local Transportation Fund, and
Avalon Housing Authority Fund, which are reported in detail in the governmental fund financial
statements. Data from the remaining governmental funds are shown in aggregate as other
non-major governmental funds. Individual fund data for each of these non-major
governmental funds is provided in the form of supplementary information in the report.

The governmental fund financial statements can be found on page 30 of this report.

Proprietary Funds are used to account for services for which the City charges external
customers or internal departments of the City. The City maintains two types of proprietary
funds: enterprise funds and internal service funds.

Enterprise funds are used to report the same functions presented as business-type activities
in the government-wide financial statements but in greater detail and with additional

 information such as a statinct of cE;Sn 1o,v:. The Ctv us enterprise funds to nccount for
its Harbor, Sewer, Saltwatei, Sola ‘i!aste, nnd Avi!cn Tran:t funds.

Internal service funds are an accounting device useb to accumulate and allocate costs
internally among the City’s various functions. The City uses three internal service funds to
account for general administration, vehicle maintenance, and the management of risks
associated with general liability insurance. Since internal service funds predominately benefit
governmental rather than business-type activities, they have been included within
governmental activities in the government-wide financial statements but combined into a
single aggregated presentation in the proprietary fund financial statements. Individual fund
data for the internal service funds is provided in the form of supplementary information in the
report.

The basic proprietary fund financial statements can be found on page 37 of this report.

Fiduciary Funds are used to account for resources held for the benefit of parties outside the
government where the City is the trustee or fiduciary. Fiduciary funds are not reflected in the
government-wide financial statements because the resources of those funds are not available
to support the City’s own programs. The accounting used for fiduciary funds is much like that
used for proprietary funds. After the dissolution of the Avalon Community Improvement
Agency (ACIA) on February 1, 2012, the non-housing assets and liabilities of the former
redevelopment agency were transferred to the Successor Agency of the ACIA (Successor
Agency) and are reported as a fiduciary fund (private-purpose trust fund).

The fiduciary fund financial statements can be found on page 43 of this report.

Governmental Activities

The City’s net position from governmental activities increased by $3.00 million for the fiscal
year ended June 30, 2024, with program and general revenues of $18.57 million exceeding
expenses of $15.57 million. The City’s net position from governmental activities had increased
by $3.05 million in the prior fiscal year ended June 30, 2023. Total revenues for governmental
activities increased by $1.73 million (10.3%) compared to the prior fiscal year. This is

  11
 primarily attributable to increases in Investment Earnings of $1.07 million. The City benefitted
from increased average cash balances from revenues exceeding expenditures over the last
two fiscal years, higher interest rates in its Local Agency Investment Fund (LAIF) investments,
and the reinvestment of maturing Certificates of Deposits and short-term United States
Treasury obligations at higher interest rates which accounts for the increases in Investment
Earnings.

Tax revenues decreased by $312 thousand (2.4%), with decreases in transient occupancy
taxes (TOT) of $450 thousand (5.4°h) and sales tax of $29 thousand (1.3%) partially offset
by increases in property tax revenues of $81 thousand (7.9°k) and other tax revenues of $86
thousand (5.8%). TOT revenues from hotels totaled $5.33 million, down 6.2% from the prior
fiscal year, and TOT from vacation rentals totaled $2.53 million, down 3.6%. Sales tax
revenues totaling $2.19 million include $770 thousand collected as a half percent (0.5%) add-
on sales tax and passed through to Catalina Island Health to subsidize the local hospital’s
operations, in addition to the special tax for hospital infrastructure replacement. Other taxes
include a four percent (4.O%) admission tax on ticketed admissions and guided tours in the
City totaling $841 thousand, $460 thousand in Property Tax in Lieu of Vehicle License Fee,
$165 thousand in franchise fees, and $108 thousand in business license taxes.

Charges for Services decreased by $127 thousand (10.3%). The decrease is largely
attributable to decreases in fees related to building and planning, including building permit
fees down $39 thousand, planning application fees down $28 thousand, and building plan
check fees down $59 thousand. Planning and building-related revenues fluctuate year-over-
year given the size of the City and level of existing development.

Operating Grants and Contributions increased by $662 thousand (22.3%) as the result of
increases from the Measure H special tax revenues for hospital infrastructure replacement
offset by decreases in Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (LACMTA)
Local Return Proposition A Discretionary revenues. The increase in the Measure H special tax
is attributable to the scheduled doubling of the per passenger tax rate compared to the prior
fiscal year. The decrease in LACMTA Local Return revenues is due to one-time operating grant
revenues received during the prior fiscal year and used to further support land transit
operations and the commuter subsidy program.

Total expenses for governmental activities increased by $1.78 million (12.9%) compared to
the prior fiscal year. Public Safety expenses increased by $235 thousand (11.1%) as the result
of contracted increases with the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department. Fire and Ambulance
expenses increased by $407 thousand (14.3%) driven by scheduled increases in salaries and
benefits of $192 thousand (8.9%) as negotiated with the respective bargaining units and
increases in internal service charges for vehicle maintenance of $78 thousand (68.8%).
Planning, Building, & Engineering decreased by $83 thousand (8.6%) due to non-recurring
planning studies contracted and completed during the prior fiscal year. Community Services
increased by $117 thousand (11.5%) driven by non-labor related operating expenses. The
decrease in Transportation expenses was the result of the one-time operating grants received
in the prior year. The increase in General Government is from expenditures related to Measure
H.

increases. Salaries and benefits increased by $288 thousand (8.6%) for business-type

respective bargaining units.

Budgetary Highlights  —  Major Governmental Funds

A comparison of budget to actual for major governmental funds is presented in the Required

adopted budget and the final budget with amendments.

The City’s General Fund is its primary source of discretionary resources for the provision of
service deemed necessary and desirable by the citizens of Avalon and the City Council. The
original budget estimated General Fund revenues of $20.86 million. Actual revenues in the
General Fund were $4.24 lower than was budgeted despite tax revenues exceeding budget
estimates by $1.39 million. The decrease in revenues compared to budget estimates was
attributable to intergovernmental revenues, which includes grant revenues, down $6.49
million from budget estimates. The City has continued to follow a conservative approach to
revenue estimation when preparing the budget, treating the post-pandemic increases as
outliers from historical trends, and adjusted appropriations accordingly. The decrease in
intergovernmental revenues is due to grant-funded reimbursements for capital expenditures
that were estimated to be incurred during the fiscal year but were delayed while additional
grant funding opportunities were pursued.

to capital expenditures $7.69 million below the final budgeted amounts. This difference was

and charges exceeded budgeted amounts by $27 thousand due to the contracted allocation
of TOT funding to Love Catalina exceeding final budget estimates. Love Catalina receives 22%
of the TOT collected by the City based on actual receipts which exceeded final budget
estimates. Similarly, General Government contract services exceeded budgeted amounts by
$623 thousand due to add-on sales tax revenues passed through to Catalina Island Health to
subsidize local hospital operations exceeding budget estimates by $70 thousand and the

Economic Outlook and Next Year’s Budget

The City of Avalon’s local economy is centered on travel and tourism. Consequently, the City’s
revenues are strongly tied to the financial health of the economy as a whole and the average
consumer’s ability and propensity for spending on leisure travel. The City’s local economy
rebounded quickly after the pandemic, with strong visitor demand increasing average lodging
rates and other taxable sales activity, which in turn increased City tax revenues. The City was
cautious in its approach to the sudden increase in visitor-driven tax revenues and gradually
restored major capital outlays, staffing, and services that had been deferred or eliminated in
response to the pandemic. As a result, the City has significantly increased its available cash
balances, particularly in the General Fund. At a national level, the Federal Reserve responded
to this post-pandemic inflation by raising short term interest rates in 2022 and 2023. The City
benefitted from these increases in rates with meaningful investment earnings during the last
fiscal year despite visitor-driven tax revenues levelling off from post-pandemic peaks.

While it is expected that the Federal Reserve will continue to lower interest rates through the
next year, the City anticipates another year of strong investment earnings while visitor-driven
revenues continue to plateau, albeit well above pre-pandemic levels. Similar to its treatment
of the post-pandemic increases in visitor-driven revenues, the City has been prudent in its
treatment of investment earnings and is not reliant on similar investment returns to fund its
operating costs in the adopted budget. The adopted budget for the next fiscal year estimates
General Fund revenues to be up 3.0% from the Fiscal Year 2023-2024 budget. The increase
in estimated revenues is largely attributable to TOT, which was budgeted at $7.50 million in
Fiscal Year 2024-2025 compared to $7.00 million budgeted and $7.87 million actual in Fiscal
Year 2023-2024. The City has continued to take advantage of this period of economic recovery
to rebuild its unrestricted fund balance. While a portion of these unrestricted funds will likely
be used to fund future planned capital outlays, the City will maintain its unassigned fund
balance of at least 50% of its General Fund operating budget in compliance with its existing
reserve policy levels.

The City has a number of major capital projects anticipated to begin construction during the
Fiscal Year 2024-2025. The projects address the rehabilitation of several existing structures
in the City and along the waterfront, including the Green Pleasure Pier and the Cabrillo Mole
Ferry Terminal. The City has been successful in its pursuit of additional grants at the state
and federal level to offset the significant construction costs further complicated by the City’s
unique geographic location. These projects focus on improving the climate resiliency of critical
infrastructure and enhancing the City’s multi-modal transportation opportunities through
sidewalk and intersection improvements and improvements to transit facilities.

   GOVERNMENTAL FUND FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

  GENERAL FUND

The General Fund has been classified as a major fund and is used to account for resources
traditionally associated with governments which are not required legally or by sound financial
management to be accounted for in another fund.

  SPECIAL REVENUE FUNDS

The Special Revenue Funds are used to account for specific revenues that are legally restricted to
expenditure for a particular purpose. The following funds have been classified as major funds:

Local TransiJortation —  This fund is used to record allocations made by the Los Angeles County
Transportation Commission for the construction of streets, roads, bikeways, pedestrian facilities as
well as the City’s transportation system as a whole.

Avalon Housincj Authority  —This fund is used to account for the activity associated with the City’s
continuing housing operations. This fund was created effective February 1, 2012 as a result of
legislation enacted by the State of California.

  NONMAJOR FUNDS

Nonmajor Funds are the aggregate of all the other governmental funds.

Harbor  —  This fund was established to account for all harbor operations.

charge fees and sewer facilities charges. This fund is used for the operation and maintenance of

  —

pumping plants and systems.

Avalon Transit This fund was established to account for the City’s fixed route, dial-a-ride, ferry

commuter subsidy, and other transportation operations.

  —

provided by one or more departments to other departments of the City and to other government
units, on a cost reimbursement basis.
